clue.text: Retired nurse enjoys distilled spirit

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the abbreviation for the nurse is read backwards

parts.note: a VAD is a nurse of the Voluntary Aid Detachment

indicators.note: distilled means processed and transformed, so the letters of enjoys are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A nurse in retirement enjoys a glass of gin or whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' turns VAD into DAV; 'distilled' rearranges ENJOYS into YJONES. 'Distilled spirit' looks like a single drink, but the spirit is a supernatural one and 'distilled' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Davy Jones is the sailors' name for the evil spirit or devil of the sea.

clue.text: With American money around, have to stop working

indicators.note: around means the abbreviation for American money surrounds the other words' letters

parts.note: dols is an abbreviation for dollars, American money
to have something is to own it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone flush with US cash feels they can quit their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' wraps the dollar abbreviation round the two middle words, splitting it after its first letter; 'With' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To down tools is the idiom for workers ceasing work, often in a strike.

clue.text: Spirits rising in freak Dover tide

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the letters are read upwards, so backwards
in means the letters lie inside the words freak Dover

explanation.surface: A strange tide at Dover brings drink washing up the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' finds AKDOV inside 'freak Dover', and 'rising' turns it upwards; 'tide' only completes the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Vodka is one of the clear distilled spirits, so it is an example of the class.

clue.text: Abroad I call for quiet, interrupting dispute over piano what an instrument!

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the dispute sits above the piano letter

parts.note: je is French for I, a word used abroad

indicators.note: interrupting means the call for quiet breaks into the word for dispute

parts.note: a war is a dispute at its most extreme
sh is the noise made to ask for quiet
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, soft

explanation.surface: A foreigner shushes a quarrel about the piano and exclaims at the instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interrupting' puts the shush into the dispute, giving WSHAR; in a down clue 'over' stacks that above the piano letter. 'What an' only adds the exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: A Jew's harp is a small twanged musical device held against the teeth.

clue.text: No hearts get, broken between Britain and Denmark

indicators.note: broken means the letters of no hearts are smashed and rebuilt in a different order

explanation.surface: Hearts are broken in a love affair spanning two countries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges NOHEARTS; 'get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The North Sea is the stretch of water lying between Great Britain and Denmark.

clue.text: Incline to put aside

explanation.surface: Leaning towards dropping something for later.
explanation.definitionFit: A seabed or land that shelves slopes gradually; to shelve a plan is to postpone it.

clue.text: Financial assistance for Ulysses

explanation.surface: Someone seeks a subsidy on behalf of a man called Ulysses.
explanation.definitionFit: A grant is money given as aid; Ulysses S. Grant was the American Civil War general and president.

clue.text: Pass ball in the middle — that's a job for a footballer

parts.note: to pass is to go, as in passing or going by

indicators.note: in the middle means only the central letters of ball are used

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Passing the ball through the centre is a midfielder's task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the middle' takes AL from BALL. 'Pass ball' reads as a football move, but PASS is GO and only the middle of BALL counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Goalie is the informal name for a goalkeeper, the team member guarding the net.

clue.text: Writer starts to insist she earns commission

parts.note: an author is a writer

indicators.note: starts to means the opening letters of the next three words are taken

explanation.surface: An author demands a fee for her commissioned work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' takes I, S, E from 'insist she earns'. 'Commission' looks like a noun, a fee, but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To commission someone is to empower or license them to act, a synonym in the verb sense.

clue.text: One engaged in diplomacy that's understood

indicators.note: engaged in means the letter for one is placed inside the word for diplomacy

parts.note: tact is skill in diplomacy with people
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A diplomat's work is all about what goes unsaid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engaged in' puts I inside TACT; 'that's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tacit is implied or agreed without being spoken aloud in words.

clue.text: He's been left with only half 26's portion

indicators.note: only half means just the first two of the four letters of with are kept

parts.note: the answer to 26 across is an old lady whose portion from her late husband's estate is her dower

explanation.surface: A bereaved man finds himself with half of what the dowager got.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only half' keeps WI from WITH. A dower is the share of a dead husband's estate kept by his widow.
explanation.definitionFit: A man left behind by the death of his wife is a bereaved husband.

clue.text: Adaptable staff, somewhat depleted, following drink around

indicators.note: following means the shortened staff comes after the turned drink
around means the word for the drink is turned back to front

parts.note: ale is a drink, beer

indicators.note: somewhat depleted means the staff word loses a little, its last letter

parts.note: a stick is a staff

explanation.surface: Flexible employees, a little short-handed, are found going round the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adaptable staff' reads as flexible workers, but 'staff' is a stick. 'around' turns the drink, 'somewhat depleted' trims the stick's last letter, and 'following' puts the stick after the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Elastic describes something able to stretch and change, so flexible and adaptable.

clue.text: Refuse a shirt with spots

parts.note: a T-shirt, so a shirt can be the letter T
a rash is an outbreak of spots

explanation.surface: Someone declines a spotty shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb, but it is the noun for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Refuse, said with the stress on the first syllable, is rubbish, which is a synonym.

clue.text: Discuss exhaustively what to do about aching tooth

definitions.text: what to do about aching tooth

explanation.surface: Talking a problem through, like getting rid of toothache.
explanation.definitionFit: To have it out is to argue a matter fully; it is also literally what you do with a painful tooth, having it pulled.

clue.text: No great shakes — though initially taking the right course

indicators.note: shakes means the letters of no great are jumbled up
initially means only the first letter of though is used

explanation.surface: Not a brilliant performer, but at least heading the right way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shakes' rearranges NOGREAT to ONTARGE; 'initially' adds T from 'though'. 'No great shakes' is an idiom for mediocre, which hides the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: On target is the idiom for being on the correct path or aim.

clue.text: The social standing of. Leonardo?

explanation.surface: A question about the rank or status of a Renaissance painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Top drawer means of the highest class socially; read as top draw-er, it is a superlative artist like Leonardo da Vinci.

clue.text: Fair punishment

explanation.surface: A just penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine weather is fair; a fine is a monetary penalty.

clue.text: Intermediate course is roughly ten metres

indicators.note: roughly means the letters of ten metres are arranged loosely into a new order

explanation.surface: A middle-distance racecourse is about ten metres long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' rearranges TENMETRES. 'Course' looks like a track, but it is a part of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Entremets is a French term for a side dish or sweet served between main parts of a meal.

clue.text: He should feel at home in Welwyn

definitions.text: He should feel at home in Welwyn

parts.words: He should feel at home in Welwyn
parts.note: Welwyn Garden City is an English new town, so its name suits a person who tends plants and flowerbeds

explanation.surface: A man who would settle happily in a Hertfordshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Welwyn Garden City is a planned town in Hertfordshire, north of London; the clue drops 'Garden City' and relies on the solver supplying it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant-tending person belongs in a garden, and Welwyn's full name is Welwyn Garden City.

clue.text: Fellow involved in robbery is a pleasure seeker.

indicators.note: involved in means the word for fellow sits inside the word for robbery

parts.note: a heist is a robbery
a don is a fellow of a college

explanation.surface: A man taking part in a hold-up does it for the thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved in' places the college fellow inside the robbery, after its first two letters. 'Fellow' looks like the man doing the robbing.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist lives for sensual enjoyment, a person always chasing delight.

clue.text: Fools give resorts backing

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the word for resorts is read backwards

parts.note: spas are health resorts

explanation.surface: Idiots supply holiday destinations with financial support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns SPAS round; 'give' is a link. 'Backing' looks like sponsorship.
explanation.definitionFit: Saps is informal slang for gullible people, a synonym for idiots.

clue.text: Peter gets a place — the winner was predictable here

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
a seat is a place to sit

explanation.surface: Peter is given a spot where the result was never in doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: In British elections a safe seat is a constituency one party always wins; 'peter' as a safe is a crossword favourite from safecracking slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A safe seat is a constituency so loyal to one party that the election outcome is known in advance.

clue.text: Jester with, say, uplifted bauble

indicators.note: in a down clue uplifted means all the pieces are read from the bottom up, so backwards

parts.note: a wag is a joker, a jester
e.g. means for example, as say does

explanation.surface: A clown holds up a cheap trinket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uplifted' turns the whole run WAGWEG upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A gewgaw is a showy trinket of little value.

clue.text: The way to get over stiffness

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
an arch is a structure built to span a gap, so to arch is to get over

explanation.surface: The route to recovering from rigid muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The way to get over' reads as a cure for stiffness, but it splits into a road abbreviation and a span.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch, the laundry substance, gives fabric rigidity, and in a figurative sense means formality.

clue.text: Dog given a medical exam was frisky.

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
to be vetted is to be examined by a vet

explanation.surface: A dog after its check-up at the vet was lively.
explanation.walkthrough: To curvet is to leap like a horse, so 'was frisky' is its past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Curvetted means leapt or capered, a playful bounding movement.

clue.text: Youngster acted peculiarly

indicators.note: peculiarly means oddly, so the letters of acted are put in a strange order

explanation.surface: A youth behaved strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peculiarly' rearranges ACTED.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a young trainee in the forces or police.

clue.text: Ring doctor about a game

parts.note: O is the ring-shaped letter
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification
re is Latin for concerning, about

explanation.surface: Phoning the doctor about a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Ombre is an old Spanish card game for three players.
explanation.definitionFit: Ombre is a seventeenth-century card game.

clue.text: Prime Minister's first -first to sound disapproving about left

indicators.note: first means the jeer around the left letter goes ahead of the minister's letter
about means the jeering word is placed around the letter for left

parts.note: boo is the noise of disapproval

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the minister is used

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister is the first to be booed when he turns left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts L inside BOO for BLOO; 'Minister's first' is M; the second 'first' puts BLOO in front of M.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloom is the peak or flowering time, as in the prime of life.

clue.text: Old lady, put on suit first

indicators.note: first means the word for suit comes ahead of the bet

parts.note: to do is to suit, as in that will do
to wager is to put money on a bet

explanation.surface: An elderly woman gets dressed, starting with her suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' looks like dressing, but it means betting on.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowager is a widow holding a title from her late husband, typically an elderly noblewoman.

clue.text: Number I and several more find offensive

parts.note: some means several, a few more

explanation.surface: Counting off one and a few others proves unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'find' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means foul-smelling or objectionable, a synonym.

clue.text: Disconcerted as a result of being heard

indicators.note: being heard means the word is spoken, so the sound replaces the spelling

parts.note: through can mean as a result of, as in through no fault of his own

explanation.surface: Someone was unsettled by what was overheard.
explanation.walkthrough: THROUGH sounds like the entered word.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw someone is to disconcert them, and the past tense fits the definition.

clue.text: Stiff paper used for book

parts.note: hard means stiff or rigid
The Times is a newspaper

explanation.surface: Thick card is used to bind a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Hard Times is a novel by Charles Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard Times is an 1854 novel by Dickens, so it is a specific instance of the class.
